2b.html:
CVD growth is a chain of gas-phase mass transport steps and thermally activated surface processes in series. For the generic reaction 2\mathrm{AB(g)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{A(s)} + \mathrm{B_2(g)} (for example \mathrm{SiH_4} \rightarrow \mathrm{Si} + 2\mathrm{H_2}):

  1. Forced convection: reactant (p_{\mathrm{react}}) and carrier gas (p_{\mathrm{inert}}) flow through the reactor at velocity U (viscous flow, 1 to 760 Torr).
  2. Diffusion across the stagnant boundary layer of thickness \delta above the hot substrate, from C_G in the bulk gas to C_S at the surface: F_1 = h_G(C_G - C_S), with h_G = D_G/\delta.
  3. Adsorption on a surface site: \mathrm{AB} \rightarrow \mathrm{AB^*}.
  4. Surface reaction: \mathrm{AB^*} \rightarrow \mathrm{A^*} + \mathrm{B^*}, flux F_2 = k_s C_S with k_s = k_0\exp(-Q_r^*/kT_{\mathrm{sub}}).
  5. Surface diffusion of the adatom \mathrm{A^*} to steps and kinks and incorporation into the film.
  6. Recombination and desorption of the by-product: \mathrm{B^*} + \mathrm{B^*} \rightarrow \mathrm{BB^*} \rightarrow \mathrm{B_2(g)}.
  7. Back-diffusion of \mathrm{B_2} across the boundary layer and convection out with the exhaust (p_{\mathrm{prod}}).

Homogeneous reaction in the gas above the substrate is unwanted: it makes particles (powder) instead of a dense film.

Rate control. In steady state F_1 = F_2, so

F = \frac{k_s h_G}{k_s + h_G}\,C_G, \qquad v = \frac{F}{N_1}

The slower step controls. At low T, k_s \ll h_G: reaction-limited, Arrhenius, independent of flow, conformal. At high T, h_G \ll k_s: transport-limited, nearly independent of T (D_G \propto T^{3/2}), sensitive to U and reactor geometry.
pts: Labelled schematic: gas flow over the heated substrate, boundary layer and the concentration profile from C_G to C_S
Step 1: forced convection of reactant and carrier gas into the deposition zone
Step 2: diffusion of reactant through the stagnant boundary layer, F_1 = h_G(C_G - C_S)
Step 3: adsorption of the reactant on surface sites (\mathrm{AB} \rightarrow \mathrm{AB^*})
Steps 4 and 5: thermally activated surface reaction (F_2 = k_s C_S, Arrhenius k_s), surface diffusion to steps and kinks, incorporation into the film
Steps 6 and 7: desorption of the by-products (\mathrm{B_2}, \mathrm{H_2}, HCl) and their diffusion and convection out of the reactor
Notes that homogeneous gas-phase reaction gives particles and is unwanted
Steps act in series: F_1 = F_2 gives F = k_s h_G C_G/(k_s + h_G); reaction-limited at low T, transport-limited at high T
2b.sketch:
• Horizontal reactor tube: gas in on the left (p_{\mathrm{react}}, p_{\mathrm{inert}}, velocity U), out on the right (p_{\mathrm{prod}}, p_{\mathrm{inert}}); heated susceptor carrying the wafer at T_{\mathrm{sub}}.
  • Magnified surface region: boundary layer of thickness \delta, reactant concentration falling linearly from C_G to C_S; arrows F_1 (across the layer) and F_2 (into the film).
  • Surface: \mathrm{AB} arriving, adsorbing as \mathrm{AB^*}, splitting into \mathrm{A^*} + \mathrm{B^*}, \mathrm{A^*} moving to a step, \mathrm{B^*} + \mathrm{B^*} \rightarrow \mathrm{BB^*} leaving as \mathrm{B_2}; number the steps 1 to 7.
  • Optional: \ln v against 1/T with the steep reaction-limited branch (low T) and the flat transport-limited branch (high T).
2b.src: Chemical vapor deposition, slides 10-12, 15-18; Ohring, The Materials Science of Thin Films, 2nd ed., pp 317-328
2b.watch:
• "Schematically discuss": the sketch carries marks; a list of steps without a diagram loses them.
  • The surface steps are activated at T_{\mathrm{sub}}, but gas diffusion follows a power law, D_G \propto T^{3/2}/P_{\mathrm{tot}}, not an Arrhenius law. That is why the high-temperature branch is nearly flat.
  • Lower total pressure (LPCVD, about 1 Torr) raises D_G and h_G, keeps the process reaction-limited and lets wafers be stacked closely in batch furnaces.
  • One deck slide writes "absorption" for the first surface step; it is adsorption.

2c.html:
Both are chemical transport reactions. The reactor has a hotter source zone and a cooler deposition zone, and the equilibrium of the reaction shifts with temperature, so material is picked up in one zone and deposited in the other.

Disproportionation. Needs a non-volatile element that forms volatile halides in two valence states, the lower-valent one being more stable at high temperature. In the hot zone the element reacts with its higher halide; in the cool zone the lower halide splits into the element (film) and the higher halide, which diffuses back:

\mathrm{2GeI_2(g)} \ \underset{600^\circ\mathrm{C}}{\overset{300^\circ\mathrm{C}}{\rightleftharpoons}}\ \mathrm{Ge(s) + GeI_4(g)}

Similarly \mathrm{Si + SiI_4 \rightleftharpoons 2SiI_2}. Used for Al, B, Ga, In, Si, Ti, Zr, Be, Cr, and for early single-crystal Si and Ge films.

Reversible transfer. The equilibrium of a reaction among different gaseous species reverses between the zones. In the GaAs chloride process, \mathrm{AsCl_3} and \mathrm{H_2} carry liquid Ga to the substrate as GaCl:

\mathrm{As_4 + As_2 + 6GaCl + 3H_2}\ \underset{850^\circ\mathrm{C}}{\overset{750^\circ\mathrm{C}}{\rightleftharpoons}}\ \mathrm{6GaAs(s) + 6HCl}

GaAs deposits at 750 °C; at 850 °C the reaction reverses and etches it. The hydride process uses \mathrm{AsH_3} and HCl instead.

DisproportionationReversible transfer
Chemistryone element changes valence: Ge(II) to Ge(0) + Ge(IV)reaction between different species (GaCl, As, \mathrm{H_2}, HCl)
Carrierown higher halide, regenerated (closed loop)external gases (\mathrm{AsCl_3} or HCl, \mathrm{H_2}); HCl exhausted
Filmselements (Ge, Si)compound semiconductors: GaAs, InP, GaP, (Ga,In)As, Ga(As,P)
Statushistorical, early epitaxyused for optoelectronic epitaxy, now displaced by MOCVD
pts: Common basis: chemical transport between a hotter source zone and a cooler deposition zone, the equilibrium shifting with temperature
Disproportionation: element with two valence states, lower-valent halide stable at high T; it splits into element and higher halide in the cool zone
Disproportionation equation \mathrm{2GeI_2 \rightleftharpoons Ge + GeI_4} with deposition at about 300 °C and pick-up at about 600 °C (or the Si iodide example)
Reversible transfer: equilibrium of a multi-species reaction reverses between zones; forward (deposition) cool, reverse (etching) hot
Reversible transfer example: GaAs chloride process, \mathrm{As_4 + As_2 + 6GaCl + 3H_2 \rightleftharpoons 6GaAs + 6HCl}, 750 °C against 850 °C
Contrast: one element changing valence with a self-regenerating carrier against different species with external carrier gases and HCl by-product
Contrast in use: elemental films (Ge, Si) against epitaxial III-V compounds (GaAs, InP)
2c.src: Ohring, The Materials Science of Thin Films, 2nd ed., pp 307-308; Chemical vapor deposition, slide 2
2c.watch:
• The slides only show pyrolysis-type reactions; this question follows Ohring section 6.2 (six reaction types), so the textbook equations are the reference.
  • In both cases the film forms in the cooler zone: heating the deposition zone reverses the reaction and etches the film.
  • Balance the GaAs equation: 6 As, 6 Ga, 6 Cl and 6 H on each side.

3a.html:
Criterion. Residual-gas molecules arrive at the substrate in parallel with the film atoms. If every one sticks (an upper bound), the impurity fraction is (sheet, Impurities):

x_i = \frac{F_i}{F_{\mathrm{dep}} + F_i} \approx \frac{F_i}{F_{\mathrm{dep}}}, \qquad F_i = 3.513\times10^{22}\,\frac{p_i\,[\mathrm{Torr}]}{\sqrt{M_i T}}\ \mathrm{cm^{-2}\,s^{-1}}

So purity needs a low impurity partial pressure and a high deposition flux.

Evaporated film

  • Deposited at 10^{-6} to 10^{-10} Torr with no working gas. At 10^{-9} Torr of \mathrm{N_2} (300 K), F_i = 3.8\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{cm^{-2}\,s^{-1}}; at one monolayer per second (F_{\mathrm{dep}} = 10^{15}) x_i \approx 0.04\%. A higher T_{\mathrm{sor}} raises F_{\mathrm{dep}} and lowers x_i.
  • Other sources: impurities in the charge, and contamination from the heater, boat or crucible (W, Mo, Ta). A water-cooled e-beam hearth and pre-evaporation behind the shutter remove them.

Sputtered film

  • Deposited in 1 to 100 mTorr of Ar after a base pressure of only 10^{-8} to 10^{-5} Torr, at rates about 100 times lower and pressures about 10^4 times higher (Ohring).
  • 10 ppm of \mathrm{O_2}, \mathrm{H_2O} or \mathrm{N_2} in Ar at 10 mTorr gives p_i = 10^{-7} Torr: F_i = 3.8\times10^{13}\ \mathrm{cm^{-2}\,s^{-1}} and x_i \approx 4\% at 10^{15}.
  • Ar is built in: energetic reflected Ar neutrals are implanted (slide 16, printed 18: gas incorporation). The plasma also desorbs water from walls, sputters fixtures (both electrodes in RF), and compound targets are only about 99.9% pure.

Conclusion. Evaporated films, especially in UHV, are purer. Sputtered films contain Ar and more O, H and N unless the base pressure is low, the Ar purified, the target pre-sputtered and a high-rate magnetron used; Al then reaches comparable purity.
pts: Purity criterion x_i = F_i/(F_{\mathrm{dep}} + F_i) with F_i \propto p_i/\sqrt{M_i T}: low impurity pressure and high deposition flux give purer films
Evaporation in high vacuum or UHV with no working gas, with a number (about 0.04% at 10^{-9} Torr and one monolayer per second, or similar); higher rate or T_{\mathrm{sor}} purer
Evaporation impurity sources from the charge and the heater, boat or crucible; e-beam with a cooled hearth or pre-evaporation as remedy
Sputtering at 1 to 100 mTorr Ar with a poorer base pressure and lower rate; impurities carried in the gas (about 4% at 10^{-7} Torr and one monolayer per second, or similar)
Ar incorporation by implanted energetic neutrals, or plasma desorption from walls and sputtering of fixtures
Conclusion that evaporated films are purer, with remedies for sputtering (low base pressure, purified Ar, pre-sputtering, magnetron)
3a.src: Evaporative deposition and vacuum systems, slides 28, 30, 39, 53; Sputter deposition, slides 4, 16; Lecture summary: evaporation and vacuum, p 6; Ohring, The Materials Science of Thin Films, 2nd ed., pp 115-117, 206, 215
3a.watch:
• x_i is an upper bound: the sticking probability of \mathrm{O_2} on many metals is 0.1 or less, but reactive metals (Ti, Ta, Al) getter \mathrm{O_2}, \mathrm{H_2O} and \mathrm{N_2} efficiently.
  • "Purity" here is chemical purity. In compositional terms sputtering wins: an alloy target reproduces its composition, while evaporation fractionates alloys.
  • Bias sputtering can resputter weakly bound gas and lower the impurity level, but a high bias implants more Ar.

3b.html:
Given: a 150 cm wide strip, so its edge is r = 150/2 = 75 cm from the centre line; two sources at \pm D from the centre line, a distance h_v below the substrate (Fig. 1); thickness tolerance 20%, read as \pm20\% of the centre thickness d_0: 0.8 \le d/d_0 \le 1.2 everywhere on the strip.

Find: the source separation 2D and the source-to-substrate distance h_v.

Solution

Step 1, why two sources. One small-area source gives d/d_0 = [1 + (r/h_v)^2]^{-2}, which falls fast. Two sources at \pm D add their profiles, so each fills the other's fall-off and the thickness stays flat over a wider band. Fig. 1 plots this sum, one curve per D/h_v.

Step 2, choose the curve. The profile must stay between 0.8 and 1.2 out to the strip edge, as far out in r/h_v as possible. From the figure, the D/h_v = 0.7 curve rises to about 1.25 near r/h_v \approx 0.6, above 1.2, so it fails. The D/h_v = 0.6 curve peaks at only about 1.1 and stays above 0.8 farthest out; the 0.5 and lower curves fall to 0.8 sooner. Choose D/h_v = 0.6.

Step 3, read the limit. From the figure, the 0.6 curve falls to d/d_0 = 0.8 at r/h_v \approx 0.97.

Step 4, size the system.

\begin{aligned} h_v &= \frac{r}{0.97} = \frac{75\ \mathrm{cm}}{0.97} = 77.3\ \mathrm{cm} \\ D &= 0.6\,h_v = 0.6 \times 77.3\ \mathrm{cm} = 46.4\ \mathrm{cm} \\ 2D &= 2 \times 46.4\ \mathrm{cm} = 92.8\ \mathrm{cm} \end{aligned}

Answer: place the sources about 93 cm apart (each about 46 cm from the centre line) and about 77 cm from the substrate. A larger h_v also meets the tolerance but wastes evaporant, so 77 cm is the minimum distance.
pts: Takes the edge distance as half the strip width, r = 75 cm, measured from the centre line
States the tolerance window used: 0.8 \le d/d_0 \le 1.2 (\pm20\%), or 0.9 to 1.1 (a 20% total band, as in the slide 50 example)
Explains that the two source profiles add, so the dip of one is filled by the other and the thickness is flat over a wider band
Rejects D/h_v = 0.7 (peak about 1.25, outside the window) and chooses D/h_v = 0.6 (peak about 1.1, widest usable band)
Reads r/h_v \approx 0.97 (0.95 to 0.98 accepted) where the 0.6 curve reaches 0.8 (or 0.87 where it reaches 0.9, on the \pm10\% reading)
h_v = 75/0.97 \approx 77 cm (or 75/0.87 = 86 cm)
2D = 2 \times 0.6 \times 77.3 \approx 93 cm, that is D \approx 46 cm (or 2D \approx 103 cm)
Notes that a larger h_v also satisfies the tolerance but wastes evaporant, so this is the minimum distance
3b.src: Evaporative deposition and vacuum systems, slides 45-47, 49-50; Standard textbook treatment
3b.watch:
• "Tolerance of 20%" is read here as \pm20\%. If the examiner meant a total band of 20% (\pm10\%, as in the slide 50 example), use 0.9 < d/d_0 < 1.1: r/h_v = 0.87, h_v = 86.2 cm and 2D = 103.4 cm. State which reading you use.
  • r is measured from the centre line, so use half the width; using 150 cm doubles h_v. D is each source's distance from the centre line; the separation is 2D.
  • A chart reading off by 0.02 in r/h_v moves h_v by about 1.5 cm, so quote "about 77 cm".
  • The chart is the sum of two small-area (cosine) sources: that model gives a peak of 1.10 and d/d_0 = 0.8 at r/h_v = 0.96 for D/h_v = 0.6 (h_v = 78 cm), consistent with the reading.

3c.html:
The value is fixed partly by regulation and partly by plasma physics.

1. Licensed frequency. A kilowatt RF supply radiates; to avoid jamming radio communication it must use a band reserved (ITU, FCC) for industrial, scientific and medical (ISM) use; 13.56 MHz is one (as are 27.12 and 40.68 MHz), so generators and matching networks are standardised on it.

2. Above about 1 MHz.

  • Heavy ions respond only up to about 1 to 3 MHz (ion plasma frequency at 10^9 to 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}). Above that they feel the mean field, so the target holds a negative self-bias and is sputtered almost continuously, while electrons (which follow up to about 0.3 to 0.9 GHz) neutralise its charge in the brief positive part of each cycle.
  • At low frequency ions follow: both electrodes sputter in turn, and an insulating target charges up. For 3 mm of \mathrm{SiO_2} at 1\ \mathrm{mA\,cm^{-2}} the face rises about 4300 V per half-cycle at 100 kHz, but only about 32 V at 13.56 MHz.
  • Oscillating electrons gain energy and ionise, so the glow needs no secondary electrons and runs at lower pressure.

3. Not much higher. The wavelength, 22 m, far exceeds the electrodes, so their voltage is uniform; matching is easy; and the self-bias, hence the rate, stays high.

Conclusion: 13.56 MHz is the lowest convenient licensed frequency in the window where electrons follow the field and ions do not.
pts: 13.56 MHz is an ISM frequency allotted (ITU or FCC) for industrial plasma use, so high RF power does not interfere with communications; equipment standardised on it
Above about 1 MHz ions cannot follow the field (ion response limited), so the target self-biases negative and is sputtered continuously; electrons follow and neutralise the charge
At low frequency both electrodes sputter alternately and an insulating target charges within a half-cycle, stopping sputtering
Electrons gain energy from the oscillating field, giving efficient ionisation without secondary electrons and lower operating pressure
Upper limit: wavelength (22 m) much larger than the electrodes, easy matching, enough self-bias; conclusion that 13.56 MHz satisfies both physics and regulation
3c.src: Sputter deposition, slide 3; Ceramic processing: thin-film deposition, slide 80; Ohring, The Materials Science of Thin Films, 2nd ed., pp 182-184, 235-238
3c.watch:
• "Fixed" points to the licensing reason; the physics only requires "above about 1 MHz", and 5 to 30 MHz would all work.
  • The ion response frequency rises with plasma density (about 10 MHz at 10^{11}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}), so the real criterion is that ions need many cycles to cross the sheath; quote "above about 1 MHz", as Ohring does.
  • The charging figures are estimates for an assumed 3 mm \mathrm{SiO_2} target (\varepsilon_r = 3.9) and 1\ \mathrm{mA\,cm^{-2}} ion current.

4a.html:
Bias sputtering. A negative DC or RF voltage (typically −50 to −300 V, against −1 to −3 kV on the target) is applied to the substrate, so ions from the plasma bombard the film while it grows. RF bias serves insulating substrates; bias works with DC, RF, magnetron and reactive sputtering.

Microscopic effects of the bombardment:

  • removal of contaminants and adsorbed gases (Ar, O, N);
  • more nucleation sites and renucleation;
  • higher adatom surface mobility and a hotter surface, so faster reaction and interdiffusion;
  • resputtering of loosely bound atoms at peaks and corners;
  • Ar trapping, with the incorporated gas fraction rising about as V_b^2.

Resulting film properties (with examples):

  • better adhesion from the first stages of growth;
  • higher density; columnar, voided structure replaced by compact fine grains (Cr), as if the film were in a higher structure zone (slides 14-15, printed 15-16);
  • better step coverage (Al) and smoother surfaces;
  • lower resistivity of metals (Ta, W, Ni, Au, Cr) and higher optical reflectivity (W, Ni, Fe);
  • changed hardness and residual stress, usually more compressive;
  • in dielectrics, higher resistivity and lower permittivity (\mathrm{SiO_2}), lower etch rate (\mathrm{Si_3N_4}).

Limits: resputtering lowers the net rate; too high a bias traps gas, damages the lattice and over-stresses the film. Bias is a cheap control of microstructure, stress and impurities (slide 5).
pts: Defines bias sputtering: negative DC or RF substrate voltage (about −50 to −300 V) so plasma ions bombard the growing film
Mechanisms: cleaning and desorption of gases, enhanced nucleation, higher adatom mobility and surface temperature, resputtering of loosely bound atoms
Gas content controlled by bias (trapped Ar about \propto V_b^2)
Structure: denser, fine-grained, columnar voids removed (Cr example)
Properties: better adhesion and step coverage, lower resistivity and higher reflectivity of metals, changed stress and hardness, dielectric property changes (any three with examples)
Drawbacks: lower net deposition rate, gas incorporation, defects and excessive compressive stress at high bias
4a.src: Sputter deposition, slides 5, 14-15; Ohring, The Materials Science of Thin Films, 2nd ed., pp 207-209, 213-214, 233-234
4a.watch:
• Bias acts on the film, not on the target; do not confuse it with the target's own negative voltage or the RF self-bias.
  • Most ions do not arrive with the full bias energy at ordinary pressures, because of charge exchange in the sheath; at low pressure they come closer to it.
  • The same question in 2023-24 (Q3a) asks for the trend with increasing bias: there the optimum and the high-bias damage carry the marks.

4b.html:
Why the magnetron is used. Magnets behind the target add a field B parallel to the surface, perpendicular to E. Electrons are trapped in \mathbf{E}\times\mathbf{B} orbits near the target, ionise far more Ar, and the discharge draws 10 to 100 times more current at a few mTorr: high rate at low pressure (slides 11-12).

How the integrity problem arises. The trapping works only where B is parallel to the surface, between the magnet poles. There the electrons drift round a closed loop and the plasma is densest, so ion bombardment, and hence erosion, is concentrated in a ring: the racetrack (slide 12: "ring-shaped erosion trench"). The groove deepens steadily while most of the target is barely eroded.

Consequences:

  1. Poor utilisation: only 10 to 30 % of the target is used before the groove nears the backing plate; going further risks burn-through and sputtering of the bonding layer or Cu plate into the film.
  2. Arcing in reactive sputtering: the racetrack stays metallic while the uneroded area is covered with insulating compound, which charges and arcs, ejecting droplets and particles.
  3. Drifting uniformity: the eroded surface moves closer to the magnets, so B and the discharge conditions change; sputtered atoms leave the sloping groove walls in a tilted lobe, altering the thickness profile and step coverage over target life.
  4. Fracture: removing metal locally releases the target's residual stresses; local tensile stress can crack it, especially brittle refractory-alloy and compound targets.
  5. Cooling loss: distortion and bombardment heating can break contact with the water-cooled backing plate, overheating or debonding the target.

Remedies: rotating (swept) magnet arrays, rotating cylindrical targets, careful target bonding, and pulsed-DC power against arcing.
pts: Magnetron principle: crossed E and B trap electrons near the target, more ionisation, higher rate at lower pressure
Origin: plasma confined where B is parallel to the surface, so erosion is localised in a ring-shaped racetrack groove that deepens with time
Low target utilisation (about 10 to 30 %), and risk of burn-through to the backing plate
In reactive sputtering the uneroded area is poisoned by insulating compound and arcs (particles in the film)
Uniformity changes over target life: surface approaches the magnets (B rises) and emission from sloped groove walls is tilted
Mechanical: release of residual stress and thermal stress can crack the target (brittle targets especially) or detach it from the cooled backing plate
Labelled sketch of magnets, field lines, plasma ring and racetrack groove
Remedy: moving or rotating magnet arrays, rotating cylindrical targets, pulsed power
4b.sketch: • Label: magnets (S N S), B field lines, plasma ring, racetrack groove, uneroded target, water-cooled backing plate.
4b.src: Sputter deposition, slides 11-12; Ohring, The Materials Science of Thin Films, 2nd ed., pp 245-247, 253-254
4b.watch:
• The question asks how the concern arises: trace it from the field geometry (B parallel to the target only in a ring) to localised erosion, then to the consequences.
  • Do not confuse target integrity with film stress; this concerns the target itself.
  • Slide 12's figure shows the target at −500 V with deionised-water cooling; cooling failure is part of the integrity problem.

5a.html:
1. Why small, pure metal particles stop conducting (4)

Two size effects remove the free carriers, even though the inside is pure metal:

  • Quantum size effect (metal-to-insulator transition). A particle of N atoms has N states per band, so the level spacing near E_F is about \delta \approx 4E_F/3N. Thermal energy lifts electrons by about k_BT; if \delta > k_BT the topmost electrons cannot reach empty states and the particle does not conduct. For Au (E_F = 5.53 eV), \delta = k_BT at 300 K for N \approx 290 atoms, about 2 nm. Smaller particles have a gap and act as semiconductors or insulators.
  • Coulomb blockade. Each particle is isolated by an insulating shell. Adding one electron costs E_C = e^2/2C, with C = 4\pi\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_r r: for r = 1 nm and \varepsilon_r = 3, E_C = 0.24 eV \approx 9k_BT. While E_C \gg k_BT and the barrier resistance exceeds h/e^2 = 25.8 kΩ, electrons cannot hop: no current below a threshold voltage, and activated conduction, \sigma \propto \exp(-E_a/k_BT), as in a semiconductor.

2. Additives to stabilise the arrangement (4)

The additive must keep the particles apart (contact restores metallic conduction), set an insulating gap and stop growth:

  • Alkanethiols (dodecanethiol on Au or Ag): a strong metal-S bond and a dense monolayer about 1.5 nm thick that fixes the tunnel gap.
  • Polymers (PVP, PVA, sodium polyacrylate): steric stabilisation and a diffusion barrier.
  • Charged ligands (citrate): electrostatic repulsion in water.
  • Silica shells or dithiol cross-linkers for a rigid spacing; oxygen-free handling keeps the core pure.

3. Energy transport without net charge transfer or tunnelling (2 × 3.5)

  • Plasmon (near-field) coupling. Light drives a localized surface plasmon on each particle. When particles are closer than about one diameter, the oscillating dipole of one drives its neighbour, so electromagnetic energy passes along the chain, a plasmonic waveguide below the diffraction limit. Electrons only oscillate inside each particle.
  • Capacitive (dipolar) coupling. Each particle-gap-particle pair is a nanocapacitor, so an AC signal passes as displacement current with zero net charge transfer. The same dipole-dipole coupling hands excitation energy to nearby dyes or dots (Förster transfer), and heat crosses the ligand matrix as phonons.

4. Industrial use (6)

  • Single-electron devices: transistors, memories and charge sensors that switch one electron at a time, with gate steps of e/C; very low power and high density.
  • Chemiresistive vapour sensors: vapour swells the ligand shell and changes the inter-particle resistance sharply (electronic noses).
  • Plasmonic devices: nanoscale optical interconnects and SERS substrates (enhancement 10^{10} to 10^{11}) for trace detection.
  • Printed electronics: stabilised Ag inks sinter at about 150 to 250 °C, thanks to melting-point depression, into conducting tracks on plastic.
pts: (1) Quantum size effect: discrete levels with spacing \delta \approx 4E_F/3N; when \delta > k_BT electrons cannot be excited, a metal-to-insulator transition (about 2 nm for Au at 300 K)
(1) Coulomb blockade of an insulated particle: E_C = e^2/2C \gg k_BT and barrier resistance above h/e^2, so no current below a threshold and activated, semiconductor-like conduction
(2) States the additive's job: prevent contact and agglomeration and set an insulating gap
(2) Names suitable additives with how they work: thiols (metal-S monolayer), polymers (PVP, PVA, polyacrylate), citrate (electrostatic), silica shell
(3) Plasmon near-field coupling passes electromagnetic energy from particle to particle while electrons only oscillate, with no net charge crossing
(3) A second route: capacitive AC coupling (displacement current), Förster-type dipole transfer, or phonon heat conduction through the matrix
(4) Single-electron transistor, memory or charge sensor, with the reason (one electron at a time, low power)
(4) Vapour sensor (chemiresistor) or SERS sensing, with the mechanism
(4) A further use explained: plasmonic waveguides or printed conductive inks sintered at low temperature
5a.sketch:
• Bulk band filled to E_F; nanoparticle levels with \delta marked and E_F in a gap.
  • I-V: zero current inside \pm e/C, steps beyond it; smeared when e^2/2C approaches k_BT.

5a.watch:
• "Relatively pure inside" points to size effects (level spacing, charging energy), not to doping or impurities.
  • The third part is open: plasmon coupling is the route the course material points to; other energy routes that need no tunnelling and no net charge flow also earn the credit.
  • \delta \approx 4E_F/3N is an order-of-magnitude estimate; gold clusters below about 2 nm do show molecule-like gaps. At 4 K the same estimate gives about 9 nm.
  • E_C depends on the radius and the shell permittivity; quote the condition e^2/2C \gg k_BT (about 0.026 eV at 300 K) if you do not remember numbers.

5b.html:
1. Relative size and atoms per particle (7)

SAXS uses the same X-ray source as XRD but records scattering at very small angles (2\theta below about 5°). It needs no long-range order: the capped metal cores scatter by their electron-density contrast with the organic matrix, and give size, shape and size distribution for 1 to 100 nm.

  • Guinier region: \ln I(q) = \ln I_0 - q^2R_g^2/3 with q = 4\pi\sin\theta/\lambda; for a sphere R = \sqrt{5/3}\,R_g. The knee moves to lower q as particles grow, so sizes compare directly.
  • Porod region (I \propto q^{-4}) gives the surface area; a structure-factor peak at q^* gives the core spacing d \approx 2\pi/q^*, hence the ligand gap.
  • WAXS/XRD on the same sample gives the crystallite size by Scherrer; equal sizes mean single-crystal particles.

Atoms per particle: N = n_{at}\,\pi D^3/6, with n_{at} = \rho N_A/M = 59\ \mathrm{nm^{-3}} for Au: about 250 atoms at 2 nm and 830 at 3 nm.

EXAFS (XAS) counts neighbours directly: the mean coordination number falls with size (12 in bulk fcc, 9.6 for a 309-atom cluster, 7.9 for 55 atoms), which gives N.

2. Detecting conducting, semiconducting or interface effects (7)

  • XPS: a metallic particle shows a Fermi edge in the valence-band spectrum; a non-metallic one shows a gap. Core levels shift with size and oxidation (Pd 3d_{5/2} near 335 eV, PdO near 337 eV), and S 2p reveals the metal-thiolate interface.
  • XANES: oxidation state and charge transfer at the interface.
  • UV-Vis or EELS low-loss: a plasmon peak means free electrons; its loss and discrete absorption onsets mean a gap.
  • Raman and SERS: ligand-metal vibrations; SERS enhancement (10^{10} to 10^{11}) needs metallic hot spots.
  • STM and transport: STM spectroscopy (dI/dV) shows the Coulomb gap; array conductivity falling with temperature is metallic, rising (\sigma \propto e^{-E_a/k_BT}) is semiconducting.
pts: (1) Names SAXS: small-angle scattering from electron-density contrast, no crystal order needed, size and size distribution of 1 to 100 nm particles
(1) Guinier analysis, I = I_0\exp(-q^2R_g^2/3) with R = \sqrt{5/3}R_g; knee at lower q for larger particles (or Porod and inter-particle peak for spacing)
(1) Atoms per particle from the volume: N = n_{at}\pi D^3/6 (about 830 for a 3 nm Au particle), or from Scherrer or WAXS size
(1) EXAFS coordination number falls with size and gives the atoms per particle
(2) XPS: Fermi edge present (metal) or absent (gap); core-level shifts for oxidation or charge transfer at the interface
(2) Optical or EELS: plasmon peak for metallic particles, discrete absorption onsets when a gap opens; XANES for charge transfer
(2) Raman or SERS for ligand-metal interface bonding and metallic hot spots
(2) STM spectroscopy or temperature-dependent conductivity: Coulomb gap, metallic against activated \sigma \propto e^{-E_a/k_BT}
5b.sketch:
• \log I against \log q: flat Guinier region, knee at q \approx 1/R_g, Porod q^{-4} fall.
  • The larger particles with the knee at lower q and a higher plateau.

5b.watch:
• "Comparable to XRD" points to X-ray scattering (SAXS, WAXS) and X-ray absorption (XAS); TEM gives sizes too, but it is not an X-ray method. Credit any sound X-ray route.
  • The Pd values are read off the XPS case study (slide 10), to about 0.5 eV.
  • Scherrer gives the crystallite size; a twinned particle looks smaller in XRD than in SAXS.
  • The coordination numbers are for perfect cuboctahedra; real particles are close.

6a.html:
Lattice analysis. MgO and NiO are both rock salt (FCC cation lattice), a = 4.212 and 4.177 Å; Ni is FCC with a = 3.524 Å. With f = (a_s - a_f)/a_f:

\begin{aligned} \text{MgO on Ni:}\quad f &= \frac{3.524 - 4.212}{4.212} = -16.3\% \\ \text{MgO on NiO:}\quad f &= \frac{4.177 - 4.212}{4.212} = -0.83\% \end{aligned}

MgO straight on the alloy would be incoherent: high \gamma_i, Volmer-Weber islands, weak bonding and spalling. NiO, the alloy's own oxide, adheres to Ni (its 15.6% misfit is taken up by misfit dislocations), and MgO matches NiO almost exactly, with the same ionic bonding and complete (Ni,Mg)O solid solubility. So NiO is used as a template.

Method

  1. Clean the blade (degrease, then \mathrm{Ar^+} sputter-etch or \mathrm{H_2} anneal).
  2. Grow a thin (about 20 to 50 nm) NiO template by brief controlled oxidation, or deposit it by ALD or MOCVD.
  3. Deposit MgO by low-pressure MOCVD (for example \mathrm{Mg(thd)_2} + \mathrm{O_2} at about 500 to 700 °C) run reaction-limited, or by ALD (\mathrm{Mg(C_5H_5)_2} and \mathrm{H_2O} pulses, about 0.1 nm per cycle) for the thinnest layers.
  4. Anneal (about 1000 °C, inert gas) to crystallise the film and interdiffuse a graded (Ni,Mg)O interface.

Why. A small, curved blade with cooling holes needs conformal coverage; line-of-sight evaporation shadows it. MgO melts at 2852 °C, so evaporating it needs an e-beam and it loses oxygen; an MgO target needs slow RF sputtering. CVD forms the oxide by a surface reaction at a moderate T_{\mathrm{sub}} that the superalloy tolerates, giving a dense, uniform, thin layer.

Expected structure

  • Alloy / NiO (semi-coherent, misfit-dislocation network) / graded (Ni,Mg)O / MgO.
  • MgO wets its own structure type, so it grows layer by layer (FvM), cube-on-cube: (001)MgO \parallel (001)NiO, [100] \parallel [100].
  • Pseudomorphic (compressed 0.83% in-plane, tetragonally distorted) up to h_c \approx 10 nm, since h_c \propto 1/f and about 100 Å at 1% (slides 25-26). Thicker MgO is semi-coherent, with misfit dislocations about b/\lvert f\rvert = 2.98/0.0083 = 360 Å (36 nm) apart when relaxed.
  • On a polycrystalline blade, local epitaxy: columnar MgO grains continue each alloy grain; on a single-crystal blade, a single-crystal film. At 700 °C, T/T_m = 973/3125 = 0.31: dense Zone T or 2 columns, not porous Zone 1.
  • Durable: MgO and Ni alloys both expand by about 13 to 15 \times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}, so the thermal strain (\alpha_{\mathrm{sub}} - \alpha_{\mathrm{film}})\Delta T is about 0.1% over 1000 K.
pts: Misfit of MgO on Ni (about -16\%, incoherent, poor adhesion) against MgO on NiO (about -0.8\%, near-perfect match), with the reason to use NiO as a template

Deposition by a conformal method, CVD or MOCVD (or ALD), with a justification: complex blade shape, line-of-sight PVD shadows, MgO too refractory to evaporate cleanly; reactive sputtering or e-beam evaporation with substrate rotation also earns this point if justified
Process sequence: cleaning, NiO template by controlled oxidation or deposition, MgO deposition in the reaction-limited regime, interdiffusion anneal
Precursors or conditions named (Mg beta-diketonate or \mathrm{Mg(C_5H_5)_2} with \mathrm{O_2} or \mathrm{H_2O}; moderate T_{\mathrm{sub}} the alloy tolerates)
Structure: layer-by-layer, cube-on-cube epitaxy of MgO on NiO; graded (Ni,Mg)O interface from complete solid solubility
Pseudomorphic up to a critical thickness of about 5 to 12 nm (h_c \propto 1/f), then semi-coherent with misfit dislocations
Local epitaxy: columnar grains continuing the alloy grains (single crystal on a single-crystal blade); dense structure at T/T_m about 0.3
Durability: matched thermal expansion (small thermal strain), strong ionic bonding at the oxide-oxide interface, high melting point
6a.src: Epitaxy and thin film growth, part 2, slides 2-9, 12-14, 25-26; Chemical vapor deposition, slides 28-32, 55-56; Sputter deposition, slides 13-15; Ohring, The Materials Science of Thin Films, 2nd ed., pp 283, 463-464; Standard textbook treatment
6a.watch:
• "Significant difference of symmetry" in the question is read as the large difference in lattice parameter between Ni (3.524 Å) and NiO (4.177 Å), although both are FCC-based.
  • A real superalloy contains Cr and Al, which oxidise preferentially to \mathrm{Cr_2O_3} or \mathrm{Al_2O_3}; NiO forms first only at high oxygen pressure, so a deposited NiO template is the safer route.
  • The sheet's h_c formula with equal moduli (b = a/\sqrt{2} = 2.98 Å, \nu = 0.18, \lvert f \rvert = 0.0083) gives about 11 nm for 60° dislocations (b_{\mathrm{eff}} = b/2) and about 4.5 nm for pure edge dislocations lying in the interface. Quote "about 5 to 12 nm".
  • Extra depth: 6 Ni cells (21.14 Å) almost match 5 MgO cells (21.06 Å), so domain-matching epitaxy of MgO directly on Ni is possible, but the interface is weaker than oxide on oxide.

6b.html:
1. Elemental composition of the slurry (10)

Constraint. Heating, dissolving or pumping to vacuum volatilises the organometallics, so the method must work on the wet slurry at room temperature and pressure. That rules out ICP-MS and ICP-OES (dissolution and plasma), TGA and DSC (heating), and SEM-EDS and XPS (high vacuum, beam heating).

Choice: X-ray fluorescence and X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) in fluorescence mode (slides 7-8), on the slurry sealed in a thin polymer-window cell.

  • X-rays penetrate the cell and the liquid, need no vacuum and no dissolution, and do not heat the sample at low dose (a cold gas stream protects it further).
  • Element identification: each element absorbs sharply at its own K or L edge and emits its own fluorescence lines. Scanning the energy across one edge excites that element alone, which separates overlapping or trace elements, the "difficult to detect" ones; synchrotron flux reaches ppm levels.
  • Bonus speciation: XANES gives the oxidation state and EXAFS the type and number of neighbours (M-C, M-O, M-S), so the organometallic form is identified, as in the Pd sulfidation study.

Acceptable alternative: freeze the slurry (cryo-fixation, as in cryo-TEM) and analyse it on a cold stage by cryo-SEM-EDS or cryo-XPS; freezing stops volatilisation.

2. The strained, coloured organometallic film (10)

Choice: confocal micro-Raman mapping (slides 30-31), with the laser tuned into the film's colour band (resonance Raman).

  • Raman shift \Delta\bar{\nu} = 1/\lambda_0 - 1/\lambda_s gives the vibrational frequencies of metal-ligand and organic bonds.
  • Strain: stretched or compressed bonds shift the peaks (tensile to lower, compressive to higher wavenumber) and broaden them.
  • Composition: new peaks and changed intensity ratios reveal departures from the nominal composition.
  • Local: the confocal spot is about 1 µm, so a map shows where strain and composition vary.
  • Colour: the colour is an electronic absorption that moves with composition. A laser inside that band enhances the chromophore modes about 10^3 to 10^6 times. UV-Vis microspectroscopy measures the colour shift itself.
  • Non-destructive, in air, little preparation; low laser power avoids heating.

Supporting methods: micro-XRD for lattice strain (but it averages over a larger spot and needs crystalline order), HRTEM with EELS at the nanometre scale (but the beam damages organics), FTIR for functional groups (coarser, about 10 µm spots).
pts: (1) Uses the constraint: rejects methods that heat or dissolve (ICP-MS or ICP-OES, TGA, DSC) and treats vacuum and beam heating as a volatilisation risk (plain SEM-EDS or XPS only with a cryo stage)
(1) Chooses XRF or XAS (fluorescence mode) on the wet slurry at ambient pressure, or cryo-fixation followed by cryo-SEM-EDS or cryo-XPS
(1) Explains element identification: element-specific absorption edges and fluorescence lines; edge-selective excitation separates trace or overlapping elements
(1) Notes that X-rays penetrate the cell, need no vacuum and deposit little heat (low dose or cold gas stream)
(1) XANES gives the oxidation state and EXAFS the neighbours, identifying the organometallic species
(2) Chooses Raman (micro-Raman mapping), explaining the inelastic shift as a vibrational fingerprint
(2) Peak shifts and broadening measure local strain; new peaks or intensity ratios reveal the composition change
(2) Spatial resolution about 1 µm for mapping the local variation; non-destructive, ambient, low laser power
(2) Links the colour to electronic absorption: resonance Raman with the laser in the colour band, or UV-Vis microspectroscopy; credit HRTEM-EELS or micro-XRD as supporting methods
(2) Justifies the choice against alternatives (XRD averages, electron beams damage organics, FTIR is coarser)
6b.src: Nano lecture 4: characterisation, slides 3, 7-8, 9, 24, 28-32; Standard textbook treatment
6b.watch:
• The question rewards the reasoning from the constraint, so state what the slurry cannot tolerate before naming the method.
  • XPS and SEM-EDS are the usual composition tools; here they fail because the sample is volatile in vacuum. Mentioning them with a cryo stage is acceptable.
  • Resonance enhancement factors vary widely with the molecule; quote the order of magnitude only.
  • The question is open-ended; any method that respects the constraints and is justified should earn the credit.

7a.html:
Idea. Carry each precursor in the phase that tolerates it, let buoyancy bring the droplets to the interface, and let them combine there slowly under gentle, pulsed IR or microwave energy. The nutrient is then made beside the microbes, with no stirring and no long diffusion path.

1. Two microemulsion carriers. Microemulsions are clear, stable, isotropic mixtures of oil, water and surfactant (slide 33).

  • Hydrophilic precursor A in reverse (w/o) droplets dispersed in the oil: water cores, denser than oil, sink.
  • Hydrophobic precursor B in direct (o/w) droplets dispersed in the water: oil cores, lighter than water, rise.
  • Each carrier matches its continuous phase, so neither bulk phase is disturbed, and A and B cannot meet in the bulk.

2. Gentle transport. Add the droplets near the interface with a slow syringe pump or a porous distributor. Settling is creeping flow (Stokes): a 1 µm droplet with a density difference of 100\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}} in water moves about 0.2 mm per hour, so there is no turbulence. Surfactant-coated droplets adsorb at the interface: A on the oil side, B on the water side, in the biofilm.

3. Trigger: slow combination.

  • Microwave (2.45 GHz) heats by dipole rotation and ionic conduction (slide 36), so the polar water cores absorb and the oil is nearly transparent: in-core heating with instant on-off (slide 38). Short, low-power pulses raise the interface only a few kelvin, which the heat-resistant microbes tolerate.
  • IR from above also works: warming the top layer keeps the warm, light fluid on top, so no convection stirs the interface.
  • The warmth fluidises the surfactant films, so A and B droplets fuse and exchange contents slowly across the interface (collision and coalescence, slide 34). Slow combination gives the target nutrient; violent shaking gives the inert isomers.

4. Control. Set the dose by droplet size (water-to-surfactant ratio), droplet concentration, the A:B ratio and the pulse duty cycle; top up as the biofilm consumes it. Use mild, biocompatible surfactants (lecithin, Tween or Span) at low concentration, so the interface itself is not emulsified.

Conclusion. The droplets act as confined nanoreactors (the kinetic approach of slide 3): the nutrient reaches the interface without bulk diffusion or mixing.
pts: Puts the hydrophilic precursor in reverse (w/o) droplets in the oil and the hydrophobic one in direct (o/w) droplets in the water
Uses buoyancy (water cores sink in oil, oil cores rise in water) with gentle, laminar transport released near the interface; no stirring
States that A and B cannot meet in the bulk, only at the interface, so violent mixing and the inert isomers are avoided
Droplets adsorb at the interface beside the biofilm, so the nutrient forms where it is needed and slow bulk diffusion is bypassed

Explains how the chosen energy source acts: microwave (dipolar and ionic coupling of the water cores, oil nearly transparent, instant on-off) or IR (absorbed in the top layer); either route earns the point
Keeps the heating gentle: low-power pulses, or IR from above for stable stratification, so no convection stirs the interface
Mild heating fluidises the surfactant films, so droplets fuse and exchange contents slowly, giving the target nutrient rather than isomers
Controls the dose: droplet size, concentration, A:B ratio and pulse duty cycle, replenished as consumed
Biocompatible surfactants at low concentration; small temperature rise within the microbes' tolerance; interface not emulsified
Concludes that the microemulsion droplets act as confined nanoreactors delivering the nutrient without disturbing the interface
7a.src: Nano lecture 5: synthesis of nanoparticles, slides 3, 33-34, 36-39, 52, 56; Standard textbook treatment
7a.watch:
• Match each carrier to its continuous phase. A direct (o/w) emulsion added to the oil would break up and disturb the interface.
  • The question is a design problem; any route that keeps the precursors apart until the interface and combines them slowly under IR or microwave energy earns the credit.
  • True microemulsion droplets (10 to 100 nm) move mainly by Brownian motion, so release them close to the interface; larger droplets settle by buoyancy.
  • The settling speed is from Stokes' law, v = 2r^2\Delta\rho g/9\eta, with r = 0.5 µm (1 µm diameter) and \eta = 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{Pa\,s}.
  • Microwaves also heat the bulk water layer, not only the droplet cores; this is why the pulses must be short and low-power (or IR from above used instead).

7b.html:
Choice: nanoimprint lithography (NIL). It patterns by mechanical moulding, not by radiation, so its resolution is set by the mould, not by a wavelength or a beam.

Why the radiation routes fail

  • X-ray: a low-Z carbon polymer absorbs X-rays weakly, so there is little exposure contrast; no lens focuses them, so a 1:1 proximity mask and a synchrotron are needed.
  • Electron beam: deposits heat and charge in an insulating polymer, causing chain scission, cross-linking, crazing and burning; it also needs vacuum and writes serially.
  • Laser: the spot is diffraction-limited, about 0.5\lambda/\mathrm{NA}: a 405 nm laser at NA 0.9 gives about 225 nm, not nanoscale.

How NIL works (slide 11)

  1. A hard Si or \mathrm{SiO_2} mould is made once by e-beam lithography. The electron beam touches only the mould, never the soft polymer.
  2. Thermal NIL: warm the polymer above its glass-transition temperature T_g and press the mould in; the polymer flows into the cavities.
  3. Cool below T_g and demould: the inverse relief stays in the polymer.
  4. A short \mathrm{O_2} reactive-ion etch removes the thin residual layer if the pattern must reach the substrate.

Why it suits a soft polymer

  • A soft, low-T_g polymer flows at modest temperature and pressure, so imprinting is easy and gentle.
  • If the polymer cannot take heat, UV-NIL uses a liquid precursor, low pressure and a quartz mould, cured by UV at room temperature.
  • An air-cushion press (slide 13) gives uniform pressure with no lateral shift, and an anti-stick (fluorosilane) layer gives clean release.
  • Features below 10 nm are replicated; the process is parallel, cheap per wafer and the mould is reusable; 3D profiles are possible (slide 12).

Alternatives for small areas: AFM scanning-probe lithography (thermal writing of sub-100 nm pits in polycarbonate, about 10 nm features, but serial), or micro-contact printing with a PDMS stamp for chemical patterns.
pts: Chooses nanoimprint lithography (thermal or UV) as mechanical replication with a rigid mould
Explains why the given methods fail: weak X-ray absorption and no lens; electron heating, scission and charging; laser spot diffraction-limited to about \lambda/2\mathrm{NA} (about 200 nm)
Resolution set by the mould, made once by e-beam lithography on Si or quartz, so the beam never touches the polymer; sub-10 nm replication
Gives the steps: heat above T_g, press, cool and demould, \mathrm{O_2} RIE of the residual layer (or UV-NIL: liquid precursor, quartz mould, UV cure)
Explains the fit to a soft polymer: flows at low temperature and pressure; UV-NIL at room temperature if heat-sensitive
Practical points: air-cushion press for uniform pressure, anti-stick layer, mould protection
Advantages: parallel, high throughput, low cost, reusable mould, 3D patterns
Mentions an alternative with its limit: AFM scanning-probe lithography (serial), micro-contact printing or polymer pen lithography
7b.src: Nano lecture 7: nanolithography, slides 3, 9-19; Lithography and microfabrication, slides 2, 11-13; Nano lecture 10: nanophotonics, slide 12; Standard textbook treatment
7b.watch:
• Slide 11 says "heat to melt polymer". For an amorphous thermoplastic it is enough to soften it above T_g (typically T_g + 50 to 90 °C); it need not melt.
  • The laser spot estimate uses the Rayleigh form R = k_1\lambda/\mathrm{NA} with k_1 = 0.5; any value of a few hundred nanometres makes the point.
  • Near-field optical (NSOM) writing beats the diffraction limit (about 20 nm, 405-L10 slide 12) and is acceptable as a second choice, but it is serial and slow.

8a.html:
Core and shell (7)

Core options

  • Superparamagnetic iron oxide (\mathrm{Fe_3O_4}): magnetic guidance, MRI tracking, magnetic hyperthermia; biodegradable to iron stores. Best choice.
  • Gold: inert, easily functionalised (Au-S), photothermal heating and imaging; a sound core when no guidance is needed, but NIR reaches only a few centimetres, and the kidney lies deeper.
  • Porous silica or polymer: large drug load, no guidance.

Magnetic or electrical core: considerations and predictions

  • Keep \mathrm{Fe_3O_4} below about 20 nm so it is superparamagnetic: no remanence, so particles do not cluster into emboli when the field is off, which matters in clot-prone patients.
  • A field gradient falls fast with depth, so external guidance to the kidney is weak; expect help from MRI-guided or implanted magnets. An AC field penetrates the whole body for hyperthermia.
  • An "electrical" (charged or conducting) core gives no steering: blood's ions screen electric fields within a nanometre. Positive surfaces activate platelets and clotting, so keep the surface neutral or slightly negative.

Shell composition and functionalisation

  • A thin silica or gold layer anchors the coating (silane or Au-S bonds).
  • A biodegradable polyester (PLGA, PLA) shell holds the drug: the kidneys hydrolyse ester bonds, so release happens mainly there (slide 10).
  • PEG outside for stealth; antibodies or ligands to a renal-tumour receptor (for example carbonic anhydrase IX).
  • Overall size about 50 to 150 nm: above about 6 nm to avoid immediate renal filtration, below 200 nm to escape phagocytes.

Viability of the four medicines (4 × 3)

MedicinePrediction and reason
NPs coated with micro-emulsion vesiclesPoor as stated. Surfactant vesicles break up when diluted in blood and leak early; synthetic surfactants can be haemolytic. Viable only as a cross-linked, PEGylated lipid coat with a ligand.
Targeted drug in vesicles only (liposomes)Viable. Biocompatible, carry hydrophilic (core) and hydrophobic (bilayer) drugs, sized by extrusion. But no guidance or tracking, leakage and liver uptake: moderate efficiency.
Core-shell functionalised NPs aloneMost viable carrier (guidance, targeting, controlled release, imaging) but not sufficient: does not treat the slow clotting or surgical wounds, and a failing kidney clears particles poorly.
NP-biomaterial mixture for wound healingViable as support. Nanoshell-protein "solder" irradiated with light seals surgical cuts without relying on clotting (slide 6). Local only, with a thermal-damage risk; not a delivery route.
pts: Analyses core options: magnetic iron oxide (guidance, MRI, hyperthermia), gold (photothermal, imaging, shallow NIR), silica or polymer (drug load)

Magnetic core: superparamagnetic below about 20 nm, no remanence or aggregation; weak field gradient at kidney depth; MRI tracking or AC hyperthermia (a reasoned choice of a gold core with no magnetic core also earns this point)
Electrical or charged core gives no steering (fields screened in blood); positive surfaces promote clotting, so neutral or slightly negative
Shell: biodegradable polyester with ester bonds hydrolysed in the kidney, on a silica or gold anchoring layer
Functionalisation: PEG for stealth, antibody or ligand to a renal-tumour receptor; size about 50 to 150 nm (above renal cutoff, below 200 nm)
Micro-emulsion-coated NPs: a verdict with its reason, for example poor because surfactant vesicles disassemble on dilution in blood and may be haemolytic
Micro-emulsion-coated NPs: the condition for viability, a cross-linked PEGylated lipid coat with a ligand
Vesicles only: viable (biocompatible liposomes, carry both drug types)
Vesicles only: limits, no guidance or tracking, leakage, liver and spleen uptake
Core-shell alone: best carrier with guidance, targeting and release
Core-shell alone: not sufficient, since clotting, wound care and clearance by a damaged kidney remain
Wound-healing mixture: viable as support, nanoshell-protein solder sealing wounds under light without clotting
Wound-healing mixture: limits, local use only, thermal damage, not a targeted delivery route

8a.watch:
• The mark split "7 + 3 × 4" is read as 7 for the core and shell design and 3 for each medicine.
  • "Serious delays with blood clots" is read as slow clotting, which makes the wound-healing mixture useful. If read as excess clotting, the same design holds: avoid cationic, aggregating particles and add an anticoagulant payload.
  • The renal filtration cutoff (about 6 nm hydrodynamic diameter) and the CA IX marker are from the wider literature; the slides give the ester-bond kidney route and the 200 nm phagocyte limit.
  • "Predict" questions reward a clear verdict with a reason for each medicine.
  • A gold core (photothermal, imaging, Au-S anchoring of the ester shell) is an equally defensible choice if argued; the magnetic core is preferred here only for guidance and MRI tracking.

8b.html:
The growth mode follows from the energy balance in Young's equation,

\gamma_s = \gamma_i + \gamma_f\cos\theta

where \gamma_s is the substrate surface energy, \gamma_f the \mathrm{WSi_2} surface energy and \gamma_i the film-substrate interfacial energy. \gamma_f is fixed by the film, so the substrate is chosen through \gamma_s and \gamma_i. \gamma_i rises with the misfit f = (a_s - a_f)/a_f: a matched, coherent interface has a low \gamma_i, an incoherent one a high \gamma_i.

(1) Atomically smooth surface: Frank-van der Merwe

Layer-by-layer growth needs wetting, \gamma_s > \gamma_i + \gamma_f (\theta \to 0). Choose a high-surface-energy substrate that bonds strongly to the silicide (low \gamma_i) with near-zero misfit, for example isostructural tetragonal \mathrm{MoSi_2} (\lvert f \rvert below about 0.3%), so little strain energy builds up. Grow slowly at a temperature high enough for adatoms to reach step edges.

(2) Islands with bare substrate between: Volmer-Weber

Island growth needs non-wetting, \gamma_s < \gamma_i + \gamma_f (\theta > 0). Choose a low-surface-energy, inert substrate with large misfit or an incoherent interface (high \gamma_i), for example amorphous \mathrm{SiO_2}. Stop before the islands coalesce.

(3) Islands on a smooth silicide layer: Stranski-Krastanov

The first strained layers must wet, \gamma_s > \gamma_{io} + \gamma_{fo}, but with a moderate misfit of a few percent (as Ge on Si, 4%). The strain energy per area, Y\varepsilon^2 h, grows with thickness; after a few monolayers 3D islands relieve it more cheaply than flat layers, leaving islands on a smooth wetting layer.

Technique and reactions

Low-pressure CVD (LPCVD) at about 0.1 to 1 Torr, run reaction-limited for uniform, conformal films:

\mathrm{WF_6(g)} + 2\,\mathrm{SiH_4(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{WSi_2(s)} + 6\,\mathrm{HF(g)} + \mathrm{H_2(g)}

or, with dichlorosilane at a higher temperature,

2\,\mathrm{WF_6} + 7\,\mathrm{SiH_2Cl_2} \rightarrow 2\,\mathrm{WSi_2} + 3\,\mathrm{SiF_4} + 14\,\mathrm{HCl}
pts: (1) Wetting condition \gamma_s > \gamma_i + \gamma_f (\theta \to 0) gives Frank-van der Merwe layer-by-layer growth
(1) Substrate with high \gamma_s and strong bonding to the silicide (low \gamma_i)
(1) Near-zero misfit (a lattice-matched substrate such as \mathrm{MoSi_2}), and slow growth with enough adatom mobility
(2) Non-wetting condition \gamma_s < \gamma_i + \gamma_f (\theta > 0) gives Volmer-Weber islands
(2) Low-\gamma_s, inert substrate (oxide such as \mathrm{SiO_2}) with large misfit or an incoherent interface (high \gamma_i)
(2) Deposition stopped before the islands coalesce, so the substrate stays exposed
(3) Stranski-Krastanov: the first strained layers wet, \gamma_s > \gamma_{io} + \gamma_{fo}
(3) Moderate misfit (a few percent): strain energy Y\varepsilon^2 h grows with thickness until 3D islands form
(3) Islands sit on a smooth wetting layer of the silicide
Names CVD (LPCVD) as the technique, with a reason (uniform, conformal, reaction-limited)
Balanced reaction \mathrm{WF_6} + 2\mathrm{SiH_4} \rightarrow \mathrm{WSi_2} + 6\mathrm{HF} + \mathrm{H_2} (or the dichlorosilane reaction)
8b.sketch:
• Three cross-sections of film on substrate: a flat continuous film (FvM); separate caps with contact angle \theta and bare substrate between them (VW); caps sitting on a thin continuous wetting layer (SK).
  • Label \gamma_s, \gamma_i, \gamma_f and \theta at the edge of one island.

8b.watch:
• The handles are \gamma_s and \gamma_i (through bonding and misfit) plus kinetics; \gamma_f belongs to the film and cannot be chosen.
  • Slide 3 notes that Young's equation is strictly valid only for liquids; use it as an energy argument for solids.
  • A large misfit does not always give islands: with strong bonding the film can stay flat and relax by misfit dislocations above the critical thickness, h_c \sim 1/f, about 100 Angstrom at 1% misfit.
  • Silane-reduced \mathrm{WSi}_x deposits Si-rich and amorphous (x above 2) and is annealed to form tetragonal \mathrm{WSi_2}. Check the balance: W 1 = 1, Si 2 = 2, F 6 = 6, H 8 = 6 + 2.
